title: Queue
tagline: FIFO queues, enqueue and dequeue, the false overflow problem in linear queues, circular queues, and dequeue as a double-ended queue.

overview.intro: A queue is a data structure for handling values in arrival order. This chapter explains what a queue is, what enqueue and dequeue do, and why a simple linear queue can suffer from false overflow. It then explains how a circular queue solves that problem by wrapping around, and it introduces the dequeue as a more flexible queue that can operate at both ends. The chapter ends by comparing queues with stacks so that the access-order difference is clear.

blocks.text: A queue is a data structure for storing a sequence of values where the first value added is the first value removed. It is often described as FIFO, which stands for first in, first out. The everyday metaphor is a waiting line: the person who arrives first is the first to be served, and new arrivals join at the back. In a queue data structure, values are added at one end, usually called the rear, and removed from the other end, usually called the front. That single rule is what makes a queue different from a stack.

A queue is not just any ordered collection. The order matters because it is fixed by arrival: the first item in is the first item out. If you want to process items in the order they arrived, a queue is the natural choice. If you want to process the most recent item first, a queue is the wrong choice because it always gives you the oldest item next. Understanding that difference is the main point of learning about queues in this syllabus.

learn.title: The basic operations: enqueue and dequeue

blocks.text: The two core operations of a queue are enqueue and dequeue. Enqueue adds a value to the rear of the queue. Dequeue removes the value at the front and returns it. There is often also a way to look at the front value without removing it, sometimes called peek or front. Just as with a stack, a queue implementation needs to know what to do when it is empty. Trying to dequeue from an empty queue is an underflow case. Many queue implementations also have a notion of being full when they use a fixed-size storage area.

items: Enqueue adds a value to the rear of the queue.
Dequeue removes and returns the front value.
Peek or front can read the front value without removing it.
Removing from an empty queue is an underflow case.
A fixed-size queue can also become full.

learn.title: The linear array queue and the false overflow problem

blocks.text: A simple way to implement a queue is with an array and two pointers, one for the front and one for the rear. As values are enqueued, the rear pointer moves forward. As values are dequeued, the front pointer moves forward. This works for a while, but it has a problem. Once values have been removed from the front, the space they used is left behind in the array, and the rear pointer can eventually reach the end of the array even though there is still empty space near the front. That is called false overflow, because the queue seems full when it is not really using all the space available.

The name false overflow is the key clue. The queue is not genuinely full in the sense of having no space at all; it only appears full because the implementation cannot use the earlier part of the array after the front has moved past it. Recognising this problem is part of understanding why a better queue implementation is needed. The syllabus expects you to know that a simple linear queue can have this limitation and that a different organization can overcome it.

learn.title: The circular queue: reusing array space

blocks.text: A circular queue fixes the false overflow problem by letting the front and rear wrap around the array instead of marching straight to the end. When the rear reaches the end of the array, it goes back to the beginning if there is room there. The same idea applies to the front when values are removed. Because the indices wrap around, the queue can keep using the same array until it is genuinely full. That makes much better use of the available space than a simple linear queue.

The word circular is descriptive: the storage behaves as if the array is arranged in a circle rather than a straight line. In a circle, after the last position comes the first position again, so moving forward from the end wraps to the start. This is the main reason a circular queue is taught: it shows how a small change in organization can remove the false overflow limitation of a linear queue without changing the basic FIFO idea.

items.text: A circular queue with five slots.
items.note: If the rear is at the last slot and the front has moved forward, the next enqueue can use an earlier empty slot because the rear wraps around.

items.text: A linear queue with the same five slots.
items.note: The same situation could leave empty slots at the front while the rear is stuck at the end.

blocks.text: A dequeue, also called a double-ended queue, extends the queue idea by allowing insertion and removal at both ends. That means you can add at the front, add at the rear, remove from the front, and remove from the rear, depending on the implementation. This makes a dequeue more flexible than a simple FIFO queue. It is still a queue-like structure, but it gives you more options about where operations happen. The syllabus mentions dequeue alongside circular queue, so you should be able to say what extra flexibility it provides.

Because a dequeue can operate at both ends, it can model a wider range of situations than a simple queue. For example, it can support adding or removing from either end when that is useful. It should not be confused with a stack, because it still has front and rear ends and still supports queue-like access. The point is that it is a more general queue, not a completely different structure.

items: A dequeue allows insertion and removal at both ends.
It is more flexible than a simple FIFO queue.
It still has a front and a rear.
It is useful when both ends matter in a problem.

items.meaning: A double-ended queue that allows insertion and removal at both ends.

learn.title: Queue versus stack: the access-order difference

blocks.text: A queue and a stack are not opposites in the sense of being unrelated; they are just two different ways of restricting access to a sequence of values. A stack removes the most recently added value first. A queue removes the least recently added value first. That difference is the whole story. If you remember which one removes the newest item and which one removes the oldest item, you can tell them apart. The names are easy to confuse because both store values in some order and both limit where you can access them.

In practice, the choice depends on the job. If you are modelling a line of people waiting, you want the first person to be served first, so you want a queue. If you are modelling a pile of work where the latest task is the next one to be handled, you want a stack. If you pick the wrong one, the program still runs, but it does the wrong thing in a way that may be hard to spot. That is why both definitions and selection reasoning matter on the examination.

learn.title: Queue in the context of the 2027 Computer Science syllabus

blocks.text: In the 2027 ISC Computer Science syllabus, the queue is part of the Data Structures section. You are expected to understand the basic idea of a queue, its enqueue and dequeue operations, the difference between a linear and a circular queue, why a circular queue is used, and what a dequeue adds. You are also expected to distinguish a queue from a stack and to understand the access-order idea behind FIFO. The emphasis is on the concept and the reason for the different designs, not on memorising one specific code template.

That means you should be able to describe enqueue and dequeue, explain false overflow and why a circular queue avoids it, say what a dequeue is, and explain when a queue is a good or poor choice. If a question goes beyond the syllabus expectations, the safest approach is to rely on the basic queue ideas and not invent extra behaviour. The syllabus topics are the ones listed here and in the broader Data Structures material on this track.
